A technology for the in situ formation of a three-layer TiNx/Ti/TiNx functional material within a single vacuum cycle is presented, together with the results of investigations of its structural and electrophysical properties.
The maximum critical power density reached∼140 MW/cm2.
CLM-MAT-0223.statement: The maximum critical power density reached approximately 140 MW/cm2.

To evaluate the long-term stability of the structures without SiOx and with a protective SiOx layer, the current bias was selected to correspond to a power level equal to 90% of the critical value.
The measurements were carried out over 24 h of continuous operation (Figure 8).
Upon reactivation, the resistance returned to the steady-state values; the mean relative deviation for the three investigated widths was 2.17% (lower panels of Figure 8).
CLM-MAT-0224.statement: Upon reactivation after cooling from a 24 h test at 90% critical power, the mean relative deviation for the three investigated widths was 2.17%.

extra_quotes: TiNx/Ti/TiNx deposition was carried out using a Triple Target Sputter Coater DST3 equipped with a single two-inch titanium target.
The layer thicknesses were determined by X-ray reflectometry (XRR) using a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer.
Film uniformity was evaluated from a sheet-resistance map,Rs, measured by the four-point probe method using a 4Dimensions 280SI system (Figure 4b).

To determine the critical power and current-density values corresponding to microbridge failure, the current–voltage characteristics of the structures were measured. A Karl Suss PM5 probe station and a Rohde&Schwarz HMP4040 programmable power supply were used.

The absence of pronounced oscillations in the XRR curve limits the reliability of determining the thicknesses of the individual layers, since the oscillation periodandamplitudecontaininformationonthelayerthicknessesandelectron-densitycontrast.

However, theR(T)calibration was performed only over the temperature range of 23–250 °C, whereas the maximum values in Figure 7b reach 730°C. Consequently, the high-temperature values were obtained by extrapolating the linear dependence and should be regarded as estimates; their accuracy may decrease due to nonlinearity ofR(T), annealing, changes in stoichiometry, or oxidation of the film.
